payload.markdown: With strategies for generating objects covered, we’re free now to look at some strategies for structuring classes and objects. payload.text: Structuring Classes to Allow Flexible Objects

blocks.text: Structuring Classes to Allow Flexible Objects

payload.code:
Way back in Chapter 3, I said that beginners often confuse objects and classes. This was
only half true. In fact, most of the rest of us occasionally scratch our heads over UML
class diagrams, attempting to reconcile the static inheritance structures they show with
the dynamic object relationships their objects will enter into off the page.
    Remember the pattern principle, “Favor composition over inheritance”? This
principle distills this tension between the organization of classes and objects. In order
to build flexibility into our projects, we structure our classes so that their objects can be
composed into useful structures at runtime.

payload.markdown: This is a common theme running through the first two patterns of this chapter. Inheritance is an important feature in both, but part of its importance lies in providing the mechanism by which composition can be used to represent structures and extend functionality.

blocks.text: This is a common theme running through the first two patterns of this chapter. Inheritance is an important feature in both, but part of its importance lies in providing the mechanism by which composition can be used to represent structures and extend functionality.

items: Classes & Objects: A class defines state and behaviour; objects are instances of that definition.
Composition: Building classes from other objects instead of inheriting from them.
Inheritance: Deriving a class from a base class to reuse and specialise its behaviour.
Interfaces: A pure contract of method signatures with no implementation.
Static & Constants: Members belonging to the class itself rather than to any one instance.
UML Class & Sequence: Standard diagrams for static structure and runtime interaction.
Abstract Classes: A partial base class that forces subclasses to complete certain methods.
Behavioral Patterns: Patterns that distribute responsibility and coordinate behaviour.
